page: Google Cloud Platform n4a-highcpu-2 is an ARM-based compute instance built on dedicated ARMv8 Neoverse-N3 physical cores operating at 3.4 GHz. The instance provisions 2 vCPUs mapped directly to 2 physical cores with one thread per core. Memory capacity is configured at 4.0 GB of RAM, establishing a 1:2 compute-optimized ratio of 2.0 GB per core. The processor subsystem includes 64 KB of L1 data cache, 2 MB of L2 cache, and 112 MB of shared L3 cache. There is no bundled local storage included, requiring external persistent disks for storage needs, and the configuration includes no GPU accelerators.

Benchmark results highlight solid single-threaded computational throughput, registering 32.88 GB/sec in single-threaded gzip compression and an average-tier score of 2063.29 in single-core stress-ng testing. Conversely, multi-core metrics reflect the two-core physical boundary, yielding 4100.66 points in multi-core stress-ng and 2297.34 in PassMark CPU tests. Memory bandwidth tests yield 39.42 GB/sec for large block writes and 39.23 GB/sec for large block reads. Database operations score 2687.44 points, while static web serving throughput measures 5.4 GB/sec and Redis SET performance achieves 4.53 million operations per second.

The primary tradeoff of the n4a-highcpu-2 is its low memory ceiling and reliance on network storage, which restricts deployment of memory-intensive datasets or high-concurrency caching. Qualitative cost efficiency centers on delivering dedicated physical execution cores without hyper-threading overhead for low-footprint compute workloads. The instance is suited for lightweight microservices, CI/CD worker nodes, single-threaded batch data transformations, and entry-level network APIs.

Multi-core capacity is physically limited by the dual-core profile, producing 4100.66 in multi-core stress-ng and 4.53 million operations per second in Redis SET operations. Memory write throughput reaches 39.42 GB/sec. The instance delivers a predictable execution environment suited for lightweight microservices, small task queues, compression pipelines, and basic web serving.
